lessons.title: Future forms and the present perfect
lessons.programRef: Form 2 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Talk about the future with will, going to and the present continuous.
Form and use the present perfect.
Choose between the simple past and the present perfect.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: English has several ways to speak about the **future**, and a special tense, the **present perfect**, that links the past to the present. Choosing the right form shows the reader whether an event is a plan, a prediction, a finished action or a result that still matters.

blocks.title: Ways of talking about the future
blocks.md:
- **will + verb:** a decision made now, a promise or a prediction: *I will help you. It will rain tomorrow.*
- **be going to + verb:** a plan already made or something we can see coming: *We are going to visit Limbe. Look at those clouds: it is going to rain.*
- **present continuous:** a fixed arrangement: *I am travelling to Bamenda on Friday.*
- **present simple:** timetables: *The bus leaves at six.*

blocks.title: The present perfect

blocks.caption: A finished time word means the simple past.
blocks.alt: A table with four rows: simple past, I lost it yesterday; present perfect, I have lost it; since followed by a point in time; for followed by a period of time.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *I have seen him yesterday* → **I saw him yesterday** (finished time).
- *She has went* → **She has gone** (use the past participle).
- *I am here since Monday* → **I have been here since Monday.**
- *If it will rain, we stay* → **If it rains, we will stay** (no will after if).
- Mixing **since** (starting point) and **for** (length): *since 2020, for six years*.

blocks.title: Example 1: plan or prediction?
blocks.statement: Choose will or going to: *Look at the dark sky! It ___ rain.* and *I forgot my pen. I ___ borrow yours.*
steps: The first sentence uses evidence we can see: **is going to**.
The second is a decision made at the moment of speaking: **will**.
blocks.answer: is going to rain; will borrow

blocks.title: Example 2: since or for
blocks.statement: Complete: *Ngum has lived in Kumba ___ 2019 and ___ seven years.*
steps: *seven years* is a **period**: **for**. Note: both sentences use has lived.

lessons.title: Subject-verb agreement (concord)
lessons.programRef: Form 2 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Make verbs agree with singular and plural subjects.
Handle tricky subjects: each, every, either, collective nouns, and, as well as.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Concord** means that the verb must **agree** with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb (*The boy runs*); a plural subject takes a plural verb (*The boys run*). The problem is finding the real subject, which may be hidden behind other words.

blocks.title: Basic rules
blocks.md:
1. **Find the subject**, not the nearest noun: *The box of mangoes **is** heavy* (subject: box).
2. **Two subjects joined by and** are plural: *Ada and Ngu **are** friends.* (But one idea: *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast.*)
3. **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody** are singular: *Each of the girls **has** a book.*
4. **Either...or / neither...nor:** the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: *Neither the teacher nor the pupils **were** present.*

blocks.title: More tricky subjects
blocks.md:
- **Collective nouns** (class, team, committee) are singular when they act as one: *The team **is** ready.* They can be plural when members act separately: *The team **are** arguing.*
- **As well as, together with, along with** do not make the subject plural: *The principal, along with two teachers, **is** coming.*
- Words such as **news, mathematics, physics** are singular: *The news **is** good.* **Scissors, trousers, police** are plural: *The police **are** here.*

items.text: Find the subject: who or what?
Is it one or more than one?
Ignore words that come in between

blocks.caption: Follow the steps before you write the verb.
blocks.alt: A flowchart: find the subject, decide one or more, ignore words in between, then choose the verb form.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *The price of tomatoes are high* → **is high** (price is the subject).
- *Each of the boys have a ball* → **has**.
- *Mathematics are difficult* → **is difficult**.
- *The news are bad* → **is bad**.
- *Neither of them are here* → **is here**.
- *One of my friends live in Buea* → **lives** in Buea (one is the subject).

blocks.title: Example 1: hidden subject
blocks.statement: Choose the correct verb: *The bunch of bananas on the table (is / are) ripe.*
steps: Find the subject: **bunch** (of bananas is only a phrase).

blocks.title: Example 2: neither...nor
blocks.statement: Choose: *Neither the principal nor the teachers (was / were) late.*
steps: With neither...nor the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: can, may, must, should and others
lessons.programRef: Form 2 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use modal verbs for ability, permission, obligation, advice and possibility.
Form questions and negatives with modals.
Use the base verb after a modal.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: **Modal verbs** (*can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would, shall*) are helping verbs that express attitude: ability, permission, obligation, advice or possibility. They have no -s in the third person and are followed by the **base verb**: *She can swim*, never *She cans swim* or *She can to swim*.

blocks.title: What each modal does
blocks.md:
- **can / could:** ability (*She can cook ndolé*), permission (informal), possibility.
- **may / might:** permission (formal: *May I come in?*) and possibility (*It may rain*).
- **must / have to:** strong obligation (*You must wear your uniform*); **mustn't** = it is forbidden.
- **should / ought to:** advice (*You should drink more water*).
- **would / could:** polite requests (*Would you open the window?*).

blocks.caption: Think about the meaning before you choose.
blocks.alt: A table matching meanings to modals: ability can, formal permission may, strong duty must, advice should, polite request could or would.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *He can to run* / *She cans sing* → **He can run, she can sing.**
- *Do you can help me?* → **Can you help me?** (the modal itself makes the question).
- *You mustn't come = you don't have to come* is **wrong**: *mustn't* means forbidden, *don't have to* means not necessary.
- *He should went* → **should go**.

blocks.title: Example 1: obligation or advice
blocks.statement: Complete with must or should: *Pupils ___ not use phones in class (school rule). You ___ revise a little every day (friendly advice).*
steps: A school rule is a strong obligation: **must**.

blocks.title: Example 2: make a question
blocks.statement: Turn into a question: *You can lend me a pen.*
steps: A modal moves before the subject to make a question.
Add *please* for politeness: *Can/Could you lend me a pen, please?*
blocks.answer: Could you lend me a pen, please?

exercises.prompt: Write five sentences about yourself. Use the present perfect with *already*, *just*, *never*, *since* and *for*. Write about school, home or your town.
